title: Geo fallback & rotational spare pools — capacity matrix and runbook
content:
Purpose:
This working sheet captures a proposed operational model for spare GPU capacity across regions (rotational hot pools + DR reserves), failover sequencing, and a lightweight runbook for cross-region recovery. The goal is to keep multi-region latency SLOs stable while limiting overall idle GPU cost and spreading wear on hardware.

Summary (one-liner):
Maintain a distributed rotational spare capacity equal to 15% nominal fleet plus a 5% cross-region DR uplift, with automated health-based routing and a manual escalation path for region-wide outages.

Context and constraints:
- Current fleet: ~4,800 A100-equivalent GPUs (mixed generations). Distribution (current steady state):
  - us-east-1: 2,000 GPUs
  - us-west-2: 1,200 GPUs
  - eu-west-1: 1,000 GPUs
  - apac-1: 600 GPUs
- Baseline utilization (30-day rolling): token-serving workloads peg at 62% average, peak 88% on Black Friday-style load tests.
- SLA: 99.9% region-level availability for hosted API endpoints; latency SLOs differ by customer tier.
- Cost sensitivity: every 1% idle GPUs ~ $Xk/mo (sensitive number in cost model, kept internal).

Principles:
1) Keep enough local hot spare to absorb transient node loss without cross-region traffic shift for up to 15 minutes.
2) Use rotational hot pools to prevent prolonged wear on a static subset of hardware.
3) Prefer automated, policy-driven routing for graceful degradation; fall back to manual for full-region outage.
4) Ensure observability and a short, tested runbook for failover validation and customer comms.

Capacity targets (proposal):
- Local hot spare: 10% of region capacity maintained hot and pre-warmed for model families most used in that region.
- Rotational buffer: additional 5% that is rotated monthly between racks/zones to equalize GPU hours.
- DR uplift: 5% cross-region reserved (not always hot; can be burst/prime on alarm).
- Effective spare budget: 15% local (10% hot + 5% rotational) + 5% cross-region = 20% planning headroom.

Numeric example (applied to current fleet):
- us-east-1 (2,000 GPUs): 10% hot = 200; 5% rotational = 100; local spare total = 300. Cross-region DR capacity to accept overflow = ~100 (target).
- us-west-2 (1,200 GPUs): hot 120 / rotational 60 / local spare 180 / cross-region target 60.
- eu-west-1 (1,000 GPUs): hot 100 / rotational 50 / local spare 150 / cross-region target 50.
- apac-1 (600 GPUs): hot 60 / rotational 30 / local spare 90 / cross-region target 30.
- Fleet-level effective spare = 960 GPUs (~20% of 4,800).

Operational model details:
- Rotational pools: designate a monthly rotation schedule by AZ/rack. Rotation process: drain low-priority batch jobs, warm model weights, run smoke traffic, validate perf, then mark as hot spare for the month. Rotation notes: avoid rotating whole AZ at once; stagger by 3-day windows.

- Hot-spare provisioning: hot spares run minimal agent workloads (health checks, small synthetic traffic) to keep kernel caches warm. Model families pinned to hot spares follow the region's top-3 most-used models by token volume.

- Cross-region DR behavior:
  - Tiered failover:
    1) Zonal or rack failure -> local kube autoscaling + hot spares absorb traffic.
    2) Region partial degradation (50%-80% capacity) -> traffic steering to other zones in same region + graceful fallback to us-west / eu depending on geo proximity.
    3) Full region outage -> automatic reroute to pre-defined partner regions using traffic weight map (us-east -> us-west primary, eu-west -> us-east / apac fallback).
  - Throttling: when overflow routes, apply per-customer throttles based on tier to protect capacity for high-tier customers.

- Automation and detection thresholds:
  - Health signal: node_unavailable > 3 nodes in 60s -> alert and start redistribution.
  - Region emergency threshold: usable_capacity < 70% of expected baseline for 2 minutes -> begin cross-region steer.
  - Auto-activation of DR reserve: only when region-level outage detected or manual enable; activation includes warming reserved model weights before reroute.

Runbook (quick steps for on-call):
1) Detection: Pager fires (region-critical). Confirm using traceroutes, mesh health, and provider console.
2) Immediate triage (first 15m): check zone failures, control-plane health, and hot-spare pool status.
3) If local absorb possible -> update incident with capacity headroom numbers; monitor for 30m.
4) If cross-region steer needed -> trigger traffic policy change (Ops Console -> Route Policies -> Apply pre-approved policy {policy-id}).
5) Enable cross-region DR reserve in staging then production; verify warm cache hit rates and end-to-end latency on canary traffic.
6) Customer comms: product-ops drafts initial incident note; send targeted comms to impacted customers if tiered throttles applied.
7) Post-incident: runbook owner schedules a 72-hour follow-up to reconcile capacity, rotate replacement hardware, and update rotational schedule.

Failure scenarios and expected RTO/RPO:
- Rack failure (N+1 loss): RTO under 15m (hot spares), RPO zero for in-flight requests (best-effort retry).
- Region outage (provider-level): target RTO 30–90m for baseline service depending on model warming; RPO up to 2m for streaming sessions (session loss possible).

Cost/benefit notes (high level):
- Keeping 20% effective spare raises monthly infrastructure spend ~8–12% (depends on spot vs reserved mix) but reduces risk of SLA breaches and costly emergency scale-ups.
- Rotational policy reduces mean time to hardware replacement and evens wear so long-term refresh costs are lower.

Metrics to track (dashboards suggested):
- Regional usable_capacity_pct (1m, 5m, 1h)
- Hot-spare-utilization_pct (target < 30% before cross-region steer)
- Model-warm-hit_rate on spares
- Cross-region-steer_count and per-policy RPS
- Cost delta vs utilization (daily)

Action items / open questions:
- [ACTIONS] Run a 2-week chaos test that simulates 30% region capacity loss and validate RTO/RPO (owner: Ava Patel, ETA: 2026-04-01).
- [ACTIONS] Confirm legal/regulatory constraints for routing EU traffic to non-EU regions for PII workloads (owner: Sofia Gomez, ETA: 2026-03-20).
- [QUESTION] Should rotational pools be billed to product vs infrastructure cost centers? (finance input needed).
- [QUESTION] Automate warm-loading of top-10 model weights in DR reserve — prioritize by per-token revenue impact.

Appendix (short notes):
- Warm vs cold reserve tradeoffs: warm reserves reduce reroute latency at cost of GPU cycles; cold reserves cheaper but require warm-up windows.
- Suggested next steps: schedule a tabletop DR drill with SRE + Product Ops, implement canary policy for cross-region routing changes, add per-customer fallback tiers to billing docs.

Notes to reviewers: This is a working document. Numbers are draft-level and intended to spark discussion; please annotate changes inline in the doc and add Jira tasks for any committed changes.
